z-ai__glm-5.2.summary:
The Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025 authorizes appropriations for the Department of Defense (DoD), military construction, defense-related activities, and the Department of State, while establishing new policies affecting military personnel, the defense industrial base, space operations, and foreign affairs.

For FY2025, the Act authorizes $167,849,488,000 for procurement and $143,768,041,000 for research, development, test, and evaluation. It grants the Secretary of Defense general transfer authority of up to $6,000,000,000 between DoD accounts, with exceptions for military personnel authorizations, and extends DoD audit requirements through 2034.

In military personnel policy, the Act allows the Secretary of the Air Force to designate eligible separated Air Force members as "honorary separated members of the Space Force." It authorizes posthumous awards of the Medal of Honor to Master Sergeant Roderick W. Edmonds and the Distinguished Service Cross to Staff Sergeant William D. Owens, and posthumously advances General John D. Lavelle to lieutenant general without additional pay. It expands the Future Servicemember Preparatory Course, expands Selective Service data sharing (effective 120 days after enactment), requires military recruiter access to secondary schools (effective one year after enactment), and mandates a program to accelerate MEPCOM medical records review within 120 days. It also authorizes reimbursement of up to $100 for medical costs during military entrance processing.

Regarding the defense industrial base, the Act makes permanent the distribution support program for contractors, extends the pilot program for streamlining awards for innovative technology projects to October 1, 2029, and requires a strategy for the solid rocket motor industrial base by March 1, 2025. It establishes an Office of Expanded Competition in the Air Force and a Counter Unmanned Aerial Systems Task Force within 30 days of enactment. It also limits funds for Army Special Operations Forces structure reductions until an assessment of affiliate relationships is submitted.

For foreign affairs and defense strategy, the Act requires plans for a Joint Force Headquarters in Japan (due 180 days after enactment), extended deterrence to the Republic of Korea (due March 1, 2025), and trilateral defense cooperation among the U.S., Japan, and ROK. It extends the Vietnam wartime accounting initiative to October 1, 2031, and requires a strategy addressing PLA malign activities within 270 days. It also modifies reporting on Chinese military companies, requiring biennial Defense Industrial Base reports starting December 31, 2026.

In space activities, the Act modifies notification requirements for foreign interference with critical national security space capabilities, extends the National Security Space Launch program to 2029, and requires the designation of a Senior Advisor for Space Command, Control, and Integration within 30 days. It authorizes Cooperative Threat Reduction funding, including $209,858,000 for biological threat reduction, available through FY2027.

The Act modifies humanitarian assistance authority to require written congressional notice before providing assistance exceeding $5,000,000. It authorizes up to $162,500,000 in transfer authority for the Lovell Federal Health Care Center and allows assistance to expedite military construction projects in Guam. It also authorizes the Secretary of the Navy to contract for a Naval Innovation Center at the Naval Postgraduate School.

For the Department of State, the Act authorizes up to 20 days of paid rest and recuperation leave and 10 days of overseas operations leave per year for employees in combat zones or high-risk posts. It requires tabletop exercises for overseas crisis response within 120 days and the establishment of an emergency response lessons learned clearinghouse within 180 days. It mandates standards to protect Department devices from foreign commercial spyware within 120 days. Additionally, it establishes a foundation for protected and conserved areas, authorizing $1,000,000 for FY2025 and up to $100,000,000 annually from FY2026 through FY2034, subject to a 2:1 non-U.S. cost-match requirement.

The “Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025” authorizes appropriations for the Department of Defense and military construction for fiscal year 2025 and enacts a broad set of policy reforms. The bill authorizes $167.8 billion for procurement, $14.3 billion for Army research, development, test, and evaluation, $59.0 billion for Army operation and maintenance, and $75.3 billion for Navy operation and maintenance, among other funding.

Servicemember quality of life provisions include new basic pay tables effective April 1, 2025, with caps tied to Executive Schedule levels. Postpartum physical fitness test and body composition assessment deferrals are expanded to cover pregnancy loss and stillbirth. Parental leave is extended to the Coast Guard Reserve, effective October 1, 2025. The cap on additional retired pay for extraordinary heroism is removed for Vietnam-era members. Various bonus and special pay authorities are extended through December 31, 2025. The Army’s operation and maintenance account includes an additional $170.8 million for quality of life initiatives.

Several major weapon system limitations and force structure requirements are imposed. The Secretary of Defense may not accept more than 30 F-35A, 9 F-35B, and 9 F-35C aircraft until certifying that numerous deficiencies—including digital twin models, software integration labs, and sustainment challenges—are being resolved. Construction of the Constellation-class frigate beyond the basic and functional design phase is restricted until 95 percent of design drawings are approved and certified. The Air Force is prohibited from retiring F-15E aircraft until September 30, 2027, with case-by-case exceptions for uneconomical repairs. KC-135 tanker aircraft in the reserve components may not be reduced, and replacement must be on a one-for-one basis unless waived. The Air Force must develop a 10-year tactical fighter force structure plan and report annually. Minimum inventory requirements are adjusted for several aircraft, including reducing the A-10 minimum from 135 to 96. Air base air defense sites must be fielded—at least four by September 30, 2027, and four per year thereafter.

In research and technology, the bill establishes a Chief Digital Engineering Recruitment and Management Officer to define the artificial intelligence workforce and requires AI education courses. Pilot programs are created for AI-driven biotechnology applications, workflow optimization at depots and in contract administration, and a Quantum Benchmarking Initiative at DARPA. An Agility Prime Transition Working Group is formed to accelerate hybrid-electric vertical takeoff and landing capabilities. A Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Task Force must update guidance for installation commanders within 120 days. The Office of Expanded Competition is established in the Air Force to counter adversarial capital flows. Fundamental research collaboration with certain foreign academic institutions is restricted, subject to a national security waiver.

Space provisions extend the National Security Space Launch program through 2029 and require seven days’ notice before modifying the Phase Three acquisition strategy. A hybrid satellite communication pilot program integrating government and commercial systems is mandated, along with a Middle East space security assessment.

Military construction authorizations are extended for numerous lapsed Guard and Reserve projects. The Naval Innovation Center is authorized at the Naval Postgraduate School. Assistance to Guam regulatory agencies is permitted to expedite construction. A federally funded research and development center must review DoD construction roles and responsibilities.

Homeland security measures include establishment of a DHS Northern Border Mission Center within one year, a government-wide study on security assessments for high-security leased space, and a GAO report on the Homeland Security Information Network. The bill also rescinds $13 million in unobligated balances from railroad unemployment insurance funds.

This bill, H.R. 5894, provides fiscal year 2024 appropriations for the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, and related agencies, funding programs and setting conditions on their use through September 30, 2024.

Under Title I (Department of Labor), the bill appropriates $2,836,808,000 for the Employment and Training Administration's Training and Employment Services, supporting programs under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) and the National Apprenticeship Act. Of this, $1,807,553,000 goes to Grants to States, including $712,000,000 for adult programs and $1,095,553,000 for dislocated workers. National programs receive $1,029,255,000, which funds a dislocated worker national reserve ($360,859,000), Native American programs ($60,000,000), migrant and seasonal farmworker programs ($97,396,000), YouthBuild ($105,000,000), ex-offender reintegration programs ($115,000,000), and apprenticeship expansion ($285,000,000). The bill redefines "low-income" eligibility for farmworker programs as family income at or below 150% of the poverty line. Separately, $30,700,000 funds Trade Act of 1974 benefits, and up to $3,921,556,000 is drawn from the Employment Security Administration Account for state unemployment insurance and employment service operations, with $84,066,000 for administration.

For the Department of Health and Human Services (Title II), appropriations include $402,341,000 for Public Health Service Act §229 border health and research activities, plus $58,028,000 from §241 funds. Within this, $28,000,000 supports minority AIDS prevention and treatment, and $40,000,000 is designated exclusively for sexual risk avoidance education emphasizing refraining from non-marital sexual activity using medically accurate, evidence-based information. Additional allocations include $196,000,000 for Medicare Hearings and Appeals, $56,238,000 for the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT, $80,000,000 for the Office of Inspector General, and $32,000,000 for the Office for Civil Rights.

The bill sets numerous HHS general provisions. It caps reception and representation spending at $50,000, limits grant-funded salaries to Executive Level II (exempting NIH), permits transfers of up to 1% between appropriations with no appropriation increased by more than 3%, and requires 15-day notice. It bars funds for advocating gun control (Sec. 210), conditions Title X family planning grants on family-participation certification and preserves state child abuse reporting requirements (Secs. 207–208), and prohibits Medicare Advantage from excluding entities that decline to provide abortions (Sec. 209). NIH may transfer up to 3% among institutes for HIV research.

The final general provisions (Secs. 529–541) establish several policy restrictions. Sec. 529 makes research, evaluation, and statistical funds for the Administration for Children and Families and the Bureau of Labor Statistics available for obligation through September 30, 2028, and authorizes use of a single Treasury account for such purposes. Several provisions prohibit the use of funds for specified purposes: promoting or advancing Critical Race Theory (Sec. 530); implementing Executive Orders 13985, 14035, and 14091 concerning racial equity and workplace diversity (Sec. 531); supporting the Wuhan Institute of Virology or laboratories controlled by China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Venezuela, or other designated foreign adversaries (Sec. 532); conducting or supporting gain-of-function research involving potential pandemic pathogens by foreign adversaries (Sec. 533); surgical procedures or hormone therapies for gender-affirming care (Sec. 534); diversity, equity, and inclusion offices, programs, or training (Sec. 535); and implementing Executive Orders 14076 and 14079 concerning reproductive healthcare access (Sec. 536).

Sec. 537 prohibits, notwithstanding federal marriage-recognition statutes, any discriminatory action against a person based on a sincerely held religious belief or moral conviction that marriage is the union of one man and one woman. "Discriminatory action" is defined to include altering federal tax treatment or assessing taxes, penalties, or payments.

The bill's provisions generally apply to the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024, with certain funds carrying specified availability periods extending into subsequent years.

google__gemini-3.5-flash.summary:
This Act makes appropriations for the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services (HHS), and Education, and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2024. It establishes funding levels for federal workforce training, public health initiatives, and administrative operations, while implementing significant policy restrictions and multi-billion-dollar rescissions.

### Department of Labor (Title I)
The Act appropriates $2,836,808,000 plus reimbursements for Training and Employment Services under the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) and the National Apprenticeship Act. This includes $1,807,553,000 for State Grants, allocating $712,000,000 for adult activities (available October 1, 2024 – June 30, 2025) and $1,095,553,000 for dislocated workers. Outlying areas are exempted from certain WIOA allocation formulas and may submit consolidated grant applications. 

National Programs receive $1,029,255,000, which includes:
*   $360,859,000 for the dislocated workers national reserve.
*   $285,000,000 for apprenticeship expansion.
*   $115,000,000 for ex-offender activities, including $30,000,000 for justice-involved youth.
*   $115,000,000 for regional and community college career training.
*   $105,000,000 for YouthBuild.
*   $97,396,000 for migrant and seasonal farmworkers, modifying WIOA to expand low-income eligibility to families at or below 150% of the poverty line.
*   $60,000,000 for Native American programs.

The Act also appropriates $30,700,000 for Trade Act of 1974 trade adjustment benefits. For State Unemployment Insurance (UI) and Employment Service Operations, it appropriates $84,066,000 from the General Fund and up to $3,921,556,000 from the Unemployment Trust Fund. This includes $3,141,635,000 for state UI laws, with an automatic trigger providing an additional $28,600,000 per workload increment if the Average Weekly Insured Unemployment exceeds 2,365,000.

### Department of Health and Human Services (Title II)
The Act provides $402,341,000 for General Departmental Management, supplemented by $58,028,000 under Public Health Service (PHS) Act § 241. Earmarks include $40,000,000 for competitive Sexual Risk Avoidance Education grants (subject to a 10% administrative cost cap) and $28,000,000 for Minority AIDS Prevention. It allocates $196,000,000 for Medicare Hearings and Appeals, $56,238,000 for the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, $80,000,000 for the Office of Inspector General, and $32,000,000 for the Office for Civil Rights.

General provisions restrict extramural salaries to Executive Level II, cap PHS evaluation taps at 2.5%, and limit official representation expenses to $50,000. The Secretary of HHS may transfer up to 1% of discretionary funds between accounts, provided no account is increased by more than 3%. PHS Act contract terminations are permitted up to 60 days post-award, or anytime if funds remain unpaid. 

Title X family planning grantees must certify they encourage family participation for minors and counsel on resisting sexual coercion; no projects may be required to refer for abortions, and providers remain subject to state child abuse reporting laws. The Act also prohibits Medicare Advantage plans from denying participation to entities that refuse to cover or refer for abortions.

### General Provisions and Funding Restrictions (Title V)
The Act establishes statistical and research funding flexibility, allowing research funds for the Administration for Children and Families, the DOL Chief Evaluation Office, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics to remain available for obligation through September 30, 2028. 

The Act implements several absolute funding prohibitions:
*   **Social and Educational Policies:** Bans funding for Critical Race Theory, Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) offices, programs, or training, and the implementation of Executive Orders 13985, 14035, and 14091.
*   **Healthcare and Research:** Prohibits funds for surgical procedures or hormone therapies for gender-affirming care, the implementation of Executive Orders 14076 and 14079 (reproductive healthcare access), and gain-of-function research involving potential pandemic pathogens in foreign adversary nations.
*   **Foreign Entities:** Prohibits direct or indirect funding to the Wuhan Institute of Virology or any laboratory owned or controlled by designated foreign adversaries, including China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, and Venezuela.

Additionally, the Act prohibits the federal government from taking "discriminatory action"—such as altering tax-exempt status, withholding grants, contracts, or federal benefits—against any person or entity acting in accordance with a sincerely held religious belief or moral conviction that marriage is or should be a union of one man and one woman.

### Rescissions
The Act permanently rescinds a total of $20,774,000,000 in unobligated balances:
*   $11,000,000,000 from the Nonrecurring Expenses Fund.
*   $9,774,000,000 from funds made available under Public Law 117-169.

The **Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024** (H.R. 7024) makes several changes to federal tax law across six areas.

**Child Tax Credit (Title I):** The bill changes how the refundable portion of the child tax credit is calculated so it is applied per qualifying child. It raises the maximum refundable amount from $1,400 to $1,800 (2023), $1,900 (2024), and $2,000 (2025), and indexes the credit for inflation beginning in 2024. Taxpayers may elect to use the prior year's earned income if it was higher. The IRS is directed to automatically recalculate credits for taxpayers who filed early 2023 returns.

**Business tax incentives (Title II):** For tax years 2022–2025, the bill restores immediate deduction of domestic research and experimental expenditures (rather than requiring amortization), extends a more favorable calculation for the business interest deduction limitation and 100% bonus depreciation through 2025/2026, and raises Section 179 expensing limits to $1,290,000 (with a $3,220,000 phaseout threshold).

**Taiwan (Title III):** It creates special tax rules (new Section 894A) reducing withholding rates and applying treaty-like "permanent establishment" concepts for qualified residents of Taiwan, contingent on Taiwan providing reciprocal benefits. It also authorizes the President to negotiate a tax agreement with Taiwan, subject to congressional notification, consultation, and approval/implementing legislation.

**Disaster relief (Title IV):** The bill extends special rules for disaster-related personal casualty losses, excludes from income certain wildfire relief payments (for disasters declared after 2014, received 2020–2025), and treats East Palestine train derailment payments as tax-free disaster relief.

**Housing (Title V):** It increases the state low-income housing credit ceiling for 2023–2025 and lowers (to 30%, under certain conditions) the tax-exempt bond financing threshold for the credit.

**Tax administration (Title VI):** It raises the information-reporting threshold from $600 to $1,000 (indexed). It also imposes new penalties on promoters of COVID-related employee retention credits, bars claims filed after January 31, 2024, and extends the assessment period to six years.

Most provisions apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 or 2023.

**Child Tax Credit (CTC) Changes**
The bill modifies the CTC for taxable years 2023 through 2025 by calculating the refundable portion on a per-child basis and incrementally increasing the maximum refundable amount from $1,800 in 2023, to $1,900 in 2024, and $2,000 in 2025. Beginning in 2024, the credit amount is adjusted for inflation. Taxpayers may also elect to use their prior-year earned income to calculate their credit if their current-year earned income is lower.

**Business and Innovation Incentives**
The bill delays the required amortization of domestic research and experimental expenditures until taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, temporarily reinstating immediate expensing for these domestic costs. It extends the allowance for depreciation, amortization, or depletion when determining business interest limitations through 2025. Additionally, it extends 100 percent bonus depreciation for qualified property placed in service through 2025 (and through 2026 for certain longer-production property) and increases the expensing limitation for depreciable business assets to $1,290,000.

**Taiwan Tax Provisions**
The bill establishes special double-taxation relief rules for qualified residents of Taiwan, reducing withholding tax rates on U.S.-source interest, dividends, and royalties, and exempting certain qualified wages from U.S. taxation. These provisions apply only if the Secretary of the Treasury determines that Taiwan provides reciprocal benefits to U.S. taxpayers. The bill also authorizes the President to negotiate and enter into a formal bilateral tax agreement with Taiwan, subject to congressional approval and implementation legislation.

The bill, titled the “Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024,” makes changes across several areas of tax law. Its primary purpose is to modify the child tax credit for working families, revive certain business tax incentives, establish a special tax framework for qualifying residents of Taiwan, provide tax relief for specific disaster victims, and adjust low-income housing credit rules.

For the child tax credit, the bill changes how the refundable portion is calculated for tax years 2023 through 2025. crs_reference.summary:
Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024 
TITLE I--TAX RELIEF FOR WORKING FAMILIES 
This title modifies the calculation of the refundable portion of the child tax credit to require the multiplication of the credit amount in calendar years 2023-2025 by the number of qualifying children. The maximum refundable amount per child of such credit is increased to $1,800 in 2023, $1,900 in 2024, and $2,000 in 2025, with an inflation adjustment beginning after 2023. 
The title allows taxpayers to elect in 2024 and 2025 to use prior year earned income in calculating their earned income tax credit 
TITLE II--AMERICAN INNOVATION AND GROWTH 
This title allows taxpayers to delay the date on which they must begin deducting their domestic research or experimental research costs over a five-year period until 2026. Taxpayers may therefore expense such costs incurred between 2022-2026. 
The title extends the allowance for depreciation, amortization, or depletion in determining the limitation of the business interest deduction. It also extends 100% bonus depreciation and increases the limitations on expensing of depreciable business assets. 
TITLE III--INCREASING GLOBAL COMPETITIVENESS 
Subtitle A--United States-Taiwan Expedited Double-Tax Relief Act 
United States-Taiwan Expedited Double-Tax Relief Act 
This subtitle sets forth special rules for the taxation of certain residents of Taiwan, including rules for the reduction of withholding taxes, the application of permanent establishment rules, the treatment of income from employment, and the determination of Taiwanese residency, including rules for dual residents. 
Subtitle B--United States-Taiwan Tax Agreement Authorization Act 
United States-Taiwan Tax Agreement Authorization Act 
This subtitle grants the President authority to negotiate and enter into a U.S.-Taiwan tax agreement after the tax provisions of this title are enacted and effective. 
TITLE IV--ASSISTANCE FOR DISASTER-IMPACTED COMMUNITIES 
Federal Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2024 
This title excludes from gross income, for income tax purposes, compensation for losses or damages due to certain wildfires. It applies only to payments received by a taxpayer after 2019 and before 2026. 
The title also excludes payment for compensation for losses or damages from the derailment of a train in East Palestine, Ohio, on February 3, 2023. 
TITLE V--MORE AFFORDABLE HOUSING 
This title increases the low-income housing tax credit ceiling to 12.5% for calendar years 2023-2025. It also lowers the bond-financing threshold to 30% for projects financed by bonds issued before 2026. 
TITLE VI--TAX ADMINISTRATION AND ELIMINATING FRAUD 
This title increases the threshold for reporting income earned by an independent contractor from $600 to $1,000, with an adjustment to the increased amount for inflation. 
The title increases penalties for aiding and abetting the understatement of tax liability with respect to the COVID-related employee retention tax credit.

prompts.judge:
You are a meticulous evaluator applying the Congressional Research Service's quality standards to a summary of a U.S. bill. CRS holds summaries to a high bar: they must be accurate, complete, neutral, and faithful to the legislative text — while also providing useful real-world context.

You are given (1) the full BILL TEXT, which is the ground truth for what the bill DOES, and (2) a SUMMARY to evaluate.

IMPORTANT — context is allowed. A good summary may include accurate real-world context that is not literally in the bill text: the common name of a program, the agency that administers it, the statute being amended, what an existing program does, etc. This is a strength, not a hallucination. Use your own knowledge and the web search tool available to you to VERIFY such contextual claims. Fail an accuracy/hallucination criterion only when a claim CONTRADICTS the bill text or is factually FALSE or fabricated — never merely because a (true) fact is absent from the bill text. Likewise, do not penalize a faithful high-level summary for omitting granular figures or minor sub-provisions, as long as it captures the bill's essential effect.

For EACH criterion below, decide:
- "applicable": true/false. For criteria marked (conditional), first decide whether the criterion is relevant to THIS bill (e.g. "Effective dates" is not applicable if the bill specifies no dates). Criteria marked (always) are always applicable.
- "pass": true/false. If applicable is false, set pass to true. Otherwise pass is true only if the summary satisfies the criterion as described.
- "why": one short sentence justifying the verdict, citing the specific issue when failing.

Be discerning: a claim that contradicts the bill or is factually wrong fails; a wrong number fails "correct_figures"; but accurate added context and reasonable high-level summarization should pass.

CRITERIA:
{criteria_block}

BILL TEXT (ground truth):
---
{bill_text}
---

SUMMARY TO EVALUATE:
---
{summary}
---

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no markdown fences, of this exact shape:
{{"verdicts": {{"<criterion_id>": {{"applicable": true, "pass": true, "why": "..."}}, ...}}}}
Include every criterion id. Output nothing else.
